input: This pricing case examines the break-even position of a SaaS tier and establishes that the tier in question breaks even at 587 units per year, when set against a current volume of 5971 units per year. The price of the tier is $321 per unit, while the variable cost is $171 per unit, which means that each unit sold makes a contribution of $150 towards the fixed costs of $88k per year. Once sales reach 587 units, the accumulated contribution is sufficient to cover the fixed costs in their entirety, and beyond that particular volume each additional unit that is sold adds its $150 of contribution to the overall result for the year. The fixed costs stand regardless of whether the tier sells anything at all, whereas the variable cost follows the volume unit by unit, so the arithmetic of the case turns on the point at which the two behaviours meet. Below the break-even volume, the contribution for the year falls short of the fixed costs, while above it, the excess contribution represents the margin that the tier earns. The volume figures used here are last year's actuals. Current volume stands well above the break-even point, at roughly ten times the volume that the fixed costs require, and the distance between the two volumes represents the fall that the tier could sustain before the fixed costs would go uncovered at the stated price and costs. It should, however, be emphasised that the case holds the price fixed: the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, and the break-even figure that has been calculated belongs specifically to the stated price. A lower price would reduce the contribution per unit, increase the volume needed in order to cover the fixed costs, and move the volume itself by an amount which the case does not attempt to quantify. Overall, on the figures as stated, the tier covers its fixed costs many times over at its current volume, and the genuinely open question is the one that the figures do not reach, namely what a change in price would do to the volume on which the entire calculation depends.
